1) Primary diagnosis
   - Post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain (PTTNP)

2) Differential diagnoses
   - Persistent idiopathic dentoalveolar pain (PIDAP)
   - Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy (PPTTN)
   - Atypical odontalgia
   - Peri-implant disease–related pain
   - Referred pain from temporomandibular disorder (TMD)

3) Clinical reasoning
   - The vignette supports a neuropathic dentoalveolar pain disorder centered in the left maxillary anterior implant region. The pain began after extraction and implant placement in the same area 4–5 years ago, is continuous, dull and aching, and is provoked by thermal stimuli and brushing. The temporal association with dental procedures is the strongest finding supporting post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain (PTTNP).
   - Temporomandibular disorder (TMD) is not supported by the examination. Maximum opening is 45 mm, there is no pain with opening or lateral movement, no deviation, no joint sounds, no locking, and no bite change. Muscle palpation scores are 0 bilaterally for masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid, occipital region, and trapezius, indicating no muscle tenderness or pain. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) palpation scores are 0 bilaterally, indicating no TMJ tenderness or pain. No familiar pain was reproduced. Under a Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD)-style framework, there is no clinical support for a primary muscle or TMJ pain disorder.
   - Persistent idiopathic dentoalveolar pain (PIDAP) is a strong differential because the pain is persistent, localized to a dentoalveolar site, and the soft tissue examination is within normal limits. It is ranked below PTTNP because the vignette includes a clear procedural onset after extraction and implant placement, which favors a post-traumatic neuropathic mechanism rather than an idiopathic one.
   - Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy (PPTTN) is closely related and highly plausible because the pain followed dental trauma/procedures in a trigeminal distribution. It is ranked just below PIDAP only because the vignette does not report objective or subjective somatosensory abnormalities such as numbness, allodynia, dysesthesia, or hypoesthesia, which would strengthen that specific neuropathy label.
   - Atypical odontalgia is included because it is a traditional label often used for persistent tooth or implant-site pain without clear odontogenic cause, especially after dental procedures. It is ranked lower because it is less specific and overlaps substantially with current neuropathic or persistent dentoalveolar pain terminology.
   - Peri-implant disease–related pain is possible because the pain is at the implant site and worsened by brushing and thermal stimuli. However, it is less likely because the soft tissue findings are within normal limits and no local inflammatory or mechanical implant findings are reported.
   - Referred pain from temporomandibular disorder (TMD) is least likely. The patient has no jaw movement pain, no joint sounds, no locking, normal mandibular range of motion, no familiar pain on muscle palpation, muscle palpation scores of 0 throughout, and TMJ palpation scores of 0 bilaterally. These findings argue strongly against TMD as the source of the maxillary pain.

4) Next steps
   - Perform a focused neurosensory examination of the left maxillary trigeminal distribution at and around the implant site, including light touch, pinprick, thermal testing, and dynamic mechanical allodynia testing, to confirm or refute a post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathic pain mechanism.
   - Obtain targeted dental and peri-implant assessment, including percussion, palpation, probing, mobility assessment as applicable, and vitality testing of adjacent teeth, to exclude a local odontogenic or peri-implant source.
   - Obtain appropriate imaging of the implant region, such as periapical radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) if indicated, to evaluate implant position and exclude local bony or dental pathology.
   - Review prior treatment records related to the extraction and implant placement to clarify the procedural timeline and any documented complications relevant to post-traumatic trigeminal injury.
   - If neuropathic pain remains most likely after local causes are excluded, refer or continue management in an orofacial pain clinic for conservative neuropathic pain management rather than additional irreversible dental treatment.
